cluster_name: Cornell gang rape allegations; NY governor appoints special prosecutor
event_summary: A Cornell University student filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was gang raped by seven fraternity members in 2024; New York Governor Kathy Hochul removed the local DA and appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor, while pledging to close a state rape-law loophole.
tldr: Across 15 countries, headline coverage almost uniformly foregrounds the institutional and legal response — special prosecutor, DA removal, law reform — rather than the underlying sexual assault, suggesting editors globally judged the governance angle more newsworthy than the crime itself. The sharpest divergence is between US and Indian outlets, where partisan framing (Trump defending the accused, Daily Wire questioning the prosecutor's independence) competes with the victim-solidarity register visible in UK and wire-service headlines ('under siege' online, #IamJaneDoe). Campus and frat-culture framing is prominent in English-language non-US press (Philippines, Singapore, UK tabloid, New Yorker) but almost absent from Latin American and French-Canadian headlines, which track the legal-institutional story alone.

single_outlet_findings.finding: The only headline in the corpus to foreground the nationality of an accused — 'Korean student among 7 sued over group sexual assault at Cornell University' — framing the story as a diaspora liability rather than an institutional failure. Every other outlet's headline avoids identifying accused by nationality.

The most editorially loaded headline in the corpus — 'Trump says I feel badly for accused Cornell gang rapists because his nemesis is investigating them' — the only title to use 'gang rapists' (not 'accused' or 'alleged attackers'), embedding a verdict while ostensibly covering Trump's political reaction.

The only headline to surface specific investigative details — ketamine, foul texts, omitted police reports, 'divided America' — that all other outlets reserved for body text. Performs tabloid disclosure at the homepage level while UK and US broadsheets kept these details below the fold.

Uniquely makes media coverage itself the story — 'What the media got right and wrong about Cornell gang rape case' — a self-reflexive meta-journalistic frame absent from every other headline in the corpus.

bottom_line: Headline coverage globally defaults to the prosecutorial and institutional frame — special prosecutor appointment, DA removal, law reform — making the state's response the visible story and the assault itself the implied background. The partisan contest (Trump attacking Letitia James, Democratic women pushing Title IX) is almost exclusively a US and Indian angle invisible in non-Anglophone press. Campus-culture framing is carried mainly by Philippine, Singaporean, UK tabloid, and US trade outlets, with the victim-solidarity signal confined to wire services and UK progressive headlines.
